title: Better than anyone expected
problem: The task was to add a small animation to the home page without any designs.
solution: I significantly improved the animation, added interaction, and optimized it with lazy loading and animation-level performance work. It ran smoothly even on older phones. I also introduced a symbolic reward for interacting with it. Although the product was not related to entertainment, the mini-game attracted many daily users and increased product engagement. Management and marketing built a summer campaign around this unexpected success, with many bloggers taking part. I turned a small animation into the summer's killer feature with millions of engaged users.
context: Summer 2024 campaign · a product with millions of users

title: Tested a new stack with a game
problem: For new projects at MTS we had to decide whether Svelte + Threlte + Pixi.js was the right stack: could it handle 3D, 2D effects and UI in one app, and how fast could we build with it.
solution: To test the stack on a real task rather than a demo, I built Alchemy Terrarium in 4 days: a browser 3D game where you gather mushrooms in a forest and brew potions from them in a cauldron in a greenhouse. The 3D scenes run on Threlte (three.js), particle effects on Pixi.js on top of the 3D, the UI and game state on Svelte 5 — all in TypeScript and SvelteKit with a static build. The stack proved itself and was adopted for new projects. Later I compressed the game's 3D models with gltf-transform and meshopt: it now loads 9.7 MB on start instead of 76.4 MB.
context: May 2026, my first month at MTS. Model weight after compression in October 2026, gzip

title: This website
problem: A portfolio of a developer whose main argument is performance. The site itself has to be the proof: 3D, animations, and interactivity — while still flying on any phone.
solution: The site was rewritten from React to SvelteKit with prerendering: every page is ready-made HTML, and the first screen ships only the JS it needs. The Threlte prism and Pixi scenes load after the page and render frames only while animating, then fall asleep at rest. The metrics in “Why me” are live measurements in the visitor's browser via the Performance API. A service worker makes the site a PWA and caches only what the visitor has already downloaded.
facts: GitHub Pages and my own metrics service in Go

title: My own programming language
problem: I wanted to write interfaces with concise Go-style syntax and strict types — without users paying for that convenience: no virtual DOM and no runtime framework in the bundle.
solution: I built MangoScript, a language with JavaScript semantics, Go-style syntax and static types that compiles to readable JavaScript. The compiler is written in TypeScript: a lexer, a parser and a type checker with generics, union types and narrowing. It reads the types of npm packages, the DOM and the standard library from TypeScript .d.ts files and writes .d.ts files for MangoScript modules, so the language works with any npm library in both directions. Components exist only at compile time: the compiler sees which nodes depend on which state and generates code that updates exactly those nodes. The language also has real goroutines, as in Go: go f(x) runs a function in a worker, a thread on a CPU core of its own, and channels and select pass data between goroutines. The compiler moves the function and everything it uses into the worker by itself and checks that it does not touch the module's mutable variables: in the example from the docs, ten goroutines count 4.5 times faster than one thread. Around the language there is a Vite plugin, a CLI, a VS Code extension and documentation written in MangoScript itself: the compiler runs right in the browser, every example has a tab with the resulting JavaScript, and there is a sandbox at the bottom.
